text: Everything in this chapter so far — unified cost, unified governance — sounds like exactly what a single product should sell you. Cloud management platforms, sometimes called brokerage layers, exist as a real tool category for that reason. This lesson covers what one genuinely adds, and the one thing it fundamentally cannot do, no matter how polished the dashboard looks.

These platforms sit above Azure, AWS, and on-prem, pulling data from each provider's own native APIs into one product — they don't replace any provider's control plane. CloudHealth, now part of VMware and Broadcom's Aria portfolio, Flexera One, and Morpheus Data are real examples of tools that occupy this space, each consuming the same billing and policy data you could query yourself.

Done well, three things are genuinely valuable: a single pane of glass for cost that automates the normalization work from Lesson 25 instead of doing it by hand every month; unified chargeback and showback reporting built on your existing tagging taxonomy; and a consolidated governance view that surfaces Azure Policy and AWS Config violations side by side, mapped to one shared control catalog.

Here's the limit that matters most. A brokerage layer cannot make Azure Blob Storage and AWS S3 operationally equivalent — different APIs, different consistency guarantees, different IAM models all remain exactly as different as before. It can put both storage costs in one chart, but it can't make migrating a real workload between them fast or risk-free, and it's itself a line item — license cost, integration upkeep, someone to own it — so adopting one is a build-versus-buy decision, not an automatic win.

With cost, governance, and the brokerage layer's real limits all on the table, the last lesson in this chapter turns to the decision that actually matters day to day: when a new workload needs a home, which cloud should it land on, and what should decide that?
